correspondences.rationale: Both denote a change in per-channel WSS attenuation that alters channel power.
Both denote frequency misalignment of a WSS passband for one channel.
Both denote hard failure of a WSS port; model A specifies the degree input port and its all-channel impact.
Both denote failure of a coherent line transmitter's laser.
Both denote a complete hardware failure of a card.
Both denote receiver-local degradation that adds a coherent-receiver penalty.
Both denote a hard physical fibre break that prevents light from passing.
Both denote an unplugged connector or patch cord that opens the optical path.
Both denote increased attenuation in a fibre span, such as from a bend or stressed cable.
Both denote increased noise contribution or noise figure from an amplifier.
Both denote an increase in differential group delay on the fibre path.
Both denote a rapid state-of-polarisation change that can exceed receiver tracking.
Both denote connector contamination that adds optical loss or penalty.
Both cover pump-laser or amplifier-unit failure resulting in no optical output.
Both denote amplifier gain falling below its configured set point.
Both denote ageing of an amplifier pump manifested as upward drive-current drift.
Both denote a non-flat amplifier gain profile across the optical band.
Both denote hard failure of an OTN switch's ODU cross-connect fabric.
Both denote an incorrectly configured OTN cross-connect that misroutes an ODU.
Both denote failure of a client port or its associated optic.
Both denote optical signal power below its expected operating level.
Model A's normal-power quality reduction is the state produced by the spectral narrowing or misalignment described in model B.
Both denote absent optical energy, including power below receiver detection.
Both denote loss of OTU frame alignment at a line receiver.
Both denote a failed equipment unit that cannot carry traffic; model B additionally states that monitoring values become invalid.
Both denote pre-FEC errors above the signal-degrade threshold while OTU framing remains aligned.
Both denote a rapid state-of-polarisation change.
Both denote degradation confined to the local receiver rather than propagated along the optical path.
Both denote reduced optical signal-to-noise ratio; model A applies it to every carried channel in its context.
Both denote section-local loss of the optical supervisory channel, which is regenerated at amplifier sites.
Both denote rising pump drive current used to maintain amplifier gain as the pump ages.
Both denote the ODU alarm-indication signal present on an ODU path.
Both denote interruption or loss of the client service.
Both denote a brief client-service interruption during protection switching.
Both denote an ODU delivered to an unintended destination by a cross-connect.
Both denote per-channel optical power measured by a ROADM channel monitor.
Both denote per-channel OSNR exposed by optical channel monitoring.
Both denote optical power measured at the line receiver input.
Both denote line errored-second counts accumulated in 15-minute bins.
Both denote pre-FEC bit error ratio at a coherent receiver.
Both denote differential group delay estimated or measured at the coherent receiver.
Both denote the rate of change of received state of polarisation.
Both denote total optical power at an amplifier input.
Both denote total optical power at an amplifier output.
Both denote pump drive current expressed as a percentage of beginning-of-life current.
Both denote client errored seconds reported in 15-minute bins.
Both denote client unavailable seconds reported in 15-minute bins.
Both denote a reconfigurable optical add/drop multiplexer based on WSS switching.
Both denote the transponder kind of coherent line interface.
Both denote the muxponder kind of coherent line interface.
Both denote an OTN line-card implementation of a line interface.
Both denote an amplifier operating at the transmitting end of an optical multiplex section.
Both denote an inline amplifier at an intermediate amplifier site.
Both denote a preamplifier at the receiving end of an optical multiplex section.
Both denote an OTN switch containing an ODU cross-connect fabric.
Both denote a generic client-facing port that maps a client signal into an ODU.
Both denote one optical wavelength channel.
Both denote every channel arriving through one ROADM degree's input port.
Both restrict impact to the particular receiver being diagnosed.
Both denote the equipment unit itself rather than its traffic.
Both denote all wavelength channels in the relevant multiplexed signal.
Both denote a proper subset of channels rather than all channels.
Both denote every ODU cross-connected through the referenced switch.
Both denote a single ODU trail or container.
Both denote the particular client service under discussion.
Both denote the local unit that raised the alarm or experienced the change.
Both denote the particular local port reporting the alarm.
Both denote the fibre span immediately upstream of and feeding the unit.
Both denote the immediately preceding optical amplifier on the signal path.
Both denote the patch or connection at the optical multiplex-section input.
Both refer to fault locations along the optical channel path before the observing receiver, though model B enumerates the upstream components more explicitly.
Both denote the remote line transmitter whose lightpath terminates at the local unit.
Both denote the remote receiver terminating the signal sent by the local unit.
Both denote the end-to-end path between the local unit and the far-end line interface.
Both denote either endpoint of the client service, with model B explicitly identifying the endpoint client ports.
Both denote an OTN switch or cross-connect located along the service's ODU path.
Both denote the working ODU path and the components on which it depends.
Both denote the protection ODU path and the components on which it depends.
Both denote the ODU path currently selected to carry the service.
Both denote baseline monitoring available across applicable units without an optional telemetry package.
Both denote availability of optical input, output, and received-power monitoring.
Both denote optional per-channel power and OSNR monitoring at ROADMs.
Both denote advanced coherent-DSP and equipment-health telemetry.
Both denote an abrupt hard failure causing traffic or signal outage.
Both denote reduced quality while traffic remains carried rather than a total outage.
Both denote a slow precursor trend before traffic is affected.
Both denote critical alarm severity.
Both denote major alarm severity.
Both denote minor alarm severity.
Both denote a reported condition with no active alarm severity.
Both denote independent per-channel ROADM switching, allowing a line-wide condition to continue on each routed channel.
